reason: The sources provide sufficient details for a surprising 45-second story with well-supported claims.
story: Discovered in 1964 when Geiger counters were shot into space on a sounding rocket, Cygnus X-1 became the very first black hole ever confirmed by science. Located roughly 7,000 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus, this stellar heavyweight is locked in a tight celestial tango with a massive blue supergiant star named HDE 226868. The two orbit each other every 5.6 days at a distance of just one-fifth the space between Earth and the sun. The black hole is constantly ripping away its companion's outer layers, forming a superheated accretion disk that blazes in X-rays. But the most mind-bending part? Cygnus X-1 is actively spewing out twin plasma jets that shine with the energy of 10,000 suns while racing outward at half the speed of light. Because these jets crash into stellar winds from the supergiant, they visibly sway back and forth like dancing beams, finally giving astronomers a front-row seat to extreme black hole physics.
angle: The first confirmed black hole in history is shooting dancing plasma jets with the energy of 10,000 suns at half the speed of light.

claims.claim: Cygnus X-1 was discovered in 1964 during a sounding rocket flight.
It is widely accepted as the first confirmed black hole.
The system is located approximately 7,000 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus.
The black hole is locked in a binary orbit with a blue supergiant star named HDE 226868.
The two objects orbit each other every 5.6 days.
The orbital separation is about 0.2 astronomical units, or one-fifth the Earth-Sun distance.
The black hole has a mass of approximately 21 times that of the sun.
The black hole continuously strips away material from its companion to form an accretion disk.
The plasma jets from Cygnus X-1 travel at about half the speed of light.
The jets shine with the equivalent energy of around 10,000 suns.
The stellar winds from the companion star cause the jets to wobble, creating 'dancing jets'.
Stephen Hawking and Kip Thorne made a famous scientific wager in the 1970s regarding whether Cygnus X-1 contained a black hole, which Hawking later conceded.

disputed: The exact spin rate of the compact object: past analysis suggested it was not rotating significantly, while later studies indicated near-maximal rotation. Scripts should attribute extreme spin rates or present them as recent findings.
